scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Rhythm of the Rain
This is Mhande. Traditional.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Mhande is a traditional Shona performance practice associated with the Karanga people of the Midlands, particularly the Shurugwi District.
It is historically tied to the mutoro rain rituals and kurova guva ceremonies, serving as an embodiment of Karanga epistemology and cultural values.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Mhande is central to the mutoro rain ritual, where it serves as a prayer for rain, and kurova guva ceremonies.
It is used to invoke majukwa rain spirits and ancestral spirits (dzavadzimu) to facilitate communication with the Creator, Mwari.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in conjunction with music, utilizing rhythmic footwork accentuated by rattles worn on the legs.
It involves stylized and coded movements that communicate historical and spiritual knowledge.
The dance is integrated with singing and hand-clapping (makwa).
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The ensemble typically features two drummers using Shauro (call) and Tsinhiro (response) drums.
Music is characterized by triple meter, cyclical structure, and polyrhythms, with a specific rhythmic pattern of '1, 2 … 1, 2, 3, 4 … 1, 2, 3.' Rattles and sometimes marimbas are also used.
Listen for the Shauro drum, Tsinhiro drum, Leg rattles, Marimbas.
The pulse is Triple meter.
A polyrhythmic soundscape driven by the call-and-response of two drums, layered with the percussive sound of leg rattles and rhythmic hand-clapping.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performances occur in both ceremonial and non-ceremonial settings, including the Matonjeni sanctuary in the Matopo Hills.
Dancers wear rattles on their legs to accentuate the rhythm of their footwork.
